The question of who has the right to govern Crimea is a subject of significant international dispute. Historically, Crimea was part of Russia until 1954 when it was transferred to Ukraine by the Soviet government. Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Crimea remained part of an independent Ukraine.

However, the situation changed dramatically in 2014. In February 2014, following the Ukrainian Revolution that ousted President Viktor Yanukovych, Russian forces took control of Crimea. This was followed in March by a controversial referendum, held under the administration of these forces, in which the majority of participants voted to join Russia. Subsequently, Russia annexed Crimea, considering it part of the Russian Federation.

The international community, including Ukraine and most United Nations member states, did not recognize the legitimacy of the referendum and the subsequent annexation. They continue to regard Crimea as part of Ukraine. Various international bodies, including the United Nations General Assembly, have reiterated their support for Ukraine's territorial integrity, considering the annexation as a violation of international law.

Therefore, while Russia administers Crimea, Ukraine and much of the international community believe that the legitimate right to govern Crimea belongs to Ukraine. The dispute remains a central element of broader tensions between Russia, Ukraine, and Western countries.
